title: Nvidia's SEC Probe Tests Market Trust in the AI Boom
from: NVIDIA FACES SEC ACCOUNTING PROBE AS TECH STOCKS SELL OFF
bottomLine: The reported SEC accounting inquiry into Nvidia is, on current evidence, an unconfirmed investigation that has been priced into a sharp, partly unrelated selloff rather than proof of fraud. Its real significance is what it exposes: heavy retail and pension exposure to a handful of AI stocks, an enforcement agency whose chair favors lighter touch, and a leadership vacuum at Nvidia that concentrates financial oversight in an interim CEO who is also CFO. Policymakers should treat disclosure quality and index concentration as the issues that matter, not the headline alone.

summary.title: The SEC probe is real in reporting but unconfirmed officially
points: Reuters reported Nov 20 that SEC enforcement staff are probing Nvidia's accounting, citing two people briefed on the matter.
The WSJ first reported an SEC probe on Nov 17 without specifying its focus; the SEC declined comment.
Reuters could not determine when the inquiry opened or whether it is a formal order of investigation.
An SEC inquiry does not establish wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action.
summary.plain: Someone with inside knowledge says the government is looking closely at Nvidia's bookkeeping. Nobody official has said so yet, and looking closely is not the same as finding a problem.

summary.title: The selloff outruns what the probe alone can explain
points: Nvidia shares fell 14% on Nov 20 and posted a seventh straight weekly decline, the longest since 2008.
Shares were already down about 6–7% before the Reuters report, pointing to other drivers.
Competing explanations include AI-spending doubts, Google and AMD competition, Huang's Nov 12 exit, and midterm-linked data-center fears.
Market-cap loss figures range from $2.5T to $2.7T depending on baseline date.
summary.plain: The stock fell a lot, but the probe news was only part of the reason. Other worries were already pushing it down, and different charts tell different stories about how much.

summary.title: Retirement savers hold more AI risk than they realize
points: Bloomberg (Nov 6) estimates about 44% of US pension holdings, roughly $610 billion, are tied to tech.
More than half of the S&P 500's gain since ChatGPT came from just 10 companies, per Bloomberg.
Nvidia reportedly made up nearly 8% of the S&P 500 before the drop, per a secondary analysis.
A University of Michigan survey tied rising consumer anxiety to a possible AI bubble.
summary.plain: Many people's retirement money is invested in index funds, and those funds hold a lot of a few big tech companies. If those companies drop, ordinary savers feel it even if they never bought a single share directly.

summary.title: Enforcement credibility depends on a lighter-touch SEC
points: SEC enforcement actions fell to 348 in FY2026 from 456, and public-company actions hit a record low of 16.
Chair Paul Atkins has said success should not be measured by case counts.
Enforcement Director David Woodcock has said the SEC is examining AI companies' disclosures.
A new financial reporting and accounting unit launched in August 2026; the 2002 Nvidia precedent ended with no penalty.
summary.plain: The referee has been blowing the whistle less often, so when it does act, people ask whether it is serious. This case will show whether the agency is tough on big companies or mostly talks about it.

summary.title: Implications for U.S. interests and policy options
points: Nvidia's 2002 and 2006–08 episodes both ended in restatement or settlement without admission; the SEC rescinded its no-admit-no-deny policy May 19, 2026.
Congressional letters seek Lutnick, Huang and Teter testimony on Dec 1, 2, 3 and 10, with subpoenas threatened.
Interim CEO Colette Kress holds both CEO and CFO roles over the numbers under review, a governance concern to flag, not a finding.
Options: insist on prompt disclosure in Nvidia's 10-Q, press the SEC for a public status statement, and examine index and pension concentration limits.
summary.plain: The government can make sure the company tells the truth quickly, that the investigators act in the open, and that people's retirement money is not overly tied to one sector. Doing nothing risks people learning the facts from rumors.

context.label: Right now
context.text: Nvidia faces a reported SEC accounting inquiry, a 46% share decline, and an interim CEO after Jensen Huang's Nov 12 resignation. Anthropic's Nov 19 Nasdaq debut has added supply and attention to the sector.

context.label: How we got here
context.text: Nvidia settled a 2002–03 SEC accounting inquiry with a no-penalty cease-and-desist order, and its 2006–08 stock-option review ended in restatement and derivative settlements. Sarbanes-Oxley created the legal framework that makes these probes possible.

context.label: The politics
context.text: Bipartisan concern runs through Congress over export controls, the Megaspeed probe, and H200 sales, with Democrats pressing on preferential treatment and Republicans urging early testimony. Public opinion is skeptical of data centers, and affordability is a midterm theme.

context.label: The people
context.text: SEC Chair Paul Atkins favors a lighter enforcement approach while touting IPO growth; Enforcement Director David Woodcock has flagged AI disclosures. Colette Kress is interim CEO and CFO, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott are central to the oversight fight.

context.label: Why now, and what's next
context.text: The probe's timing, Nvidia's 10-Q due in the coming weeks, congressional interviews on Dec 1–3, and Lutnick's Dec 10 testimony all fall in the next month. Anthropic's lockup and index-inclusion timing could add further pressure.

context.label: The culture and the public
context.text: Public sentiment is wary of AI's costs, from data centers to job displacement, while retail investors remain heavily exposed through index funds. The story reads as either a bubble warning or a routine market correction, depending on the outlet.

sections.title: The SEC probe is real in reporting but unconfirmed officially
paragraphs: The reporting that the Securities and Exchange Commission is examining Nvidia's accounting rests on anonymous sourcing. Reuters reported on November 20, 2026 that SEC enforcement staff are probing the company's accounting, citing two people briefed on the matter. The SEC declined to comment, and Nvidia did not immediately respond. The Wall Street Journal had reported an SEC probe on November 17 without specifying its focus. Those two reports are the entire public basis for the claim. No SEC statement, docket entry, filing or company disclosure confirms it.

Several basic questions remain open. Reuters could not determine when the inquiry began. It could not establish whether the matter is a formal order of investigation with subpoena power or an earlier-stage inquiry, and it could not confirm the precise accounting issues involved. The Journal's report that the probe covers whether disclosures misled investors was not corroborated by Reuters. Officials should treat each of these as unknown rather than fill the gaps with the most dramatic version in circulation.

The history cuts both ways. Nvidia was examined over its accounting in 2002, and that inquiry ended in 2003 with a cease-and-desist order issued without admission or denial and no penalty, according to the company's own 8-K. A current inquiry does not automatically resemble that one, and the SEC's rescission of its no-admit-no-deny policy on May 19, 2026 means any eventual resolution would likely take a different form. The agency's enforcement numbers are also read differently. Its chair, Paul Atkins, has said success should not be measured by case counts, while critics see a record low in public-company actions as a sign of retreat.

Officials should therefore not assume a formal enforcement case exists until the SEC says so or a filing discloses it. An inquiry does not establish wrongdoing, and many close without action. The useful signal to watch is whether Nvidia's forthcoming 10-Q describes the matter as a legal proceeding, and whether the agency itself makes any statement.
sections.why: a rumored case treated as a settled one would distort both market expectations and the policy response, while a real inquiry that is ignored would weaken public confidence in the agency's accounting enforcement.

sections.title: The selloff outruns what the probe alone can explain
paragraphs: Attributing Nvidia's slide mainly to the SEC report is an overreach. Reuters' Nov. 20 story, which cited two people briefed on the matter, did not arrive in a quiet market. Nvidia had already fallen roughly 6 to 7 percent before it published, according to Investing.com and Ynet, so part of the decline predates the news. No attribution study exists, and no official or outlet has measured how much of the 14 percent Friday drop reflects the probe, the Huang succession, Google and AMD competition, AI-spending doubts, rate expectations, or the midterm-linked fear that data-center construction would slow. CNBC and Bloomberg emphasize different mixes of these drivers, and the honest reading is that the probe is one input among several.

The loss figures disagree mainly because of baseline and timing. CNBC's Nov. 20 close showed a 14 percent Friday fall and a 46 percent decline over the period, shedding about $2.6 trillion in market capitalization. Superpower Daily's 44 percent and $2.5 trillion figures reflect an intraday read, and Yahoo Finance's $2.7 trillion headline uses a different starting point. Officials should use the Nov. 20 close as the reference, state the baseline date explicitly, and avoid quoting any single intraday or aggregator number as settled.

Context shapes how much weight the drop deserves. Nvidia's seventh straight weekly decline is its longest since 2008, but the company reported a $115.8 billion quarter on Nov. 17 and guided to roughly 75 percent growth, which cuts against a narrative of collapsing fundamentals. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, leaving Colette Kress as interim CEO, and some analysts expect a long interim period. Those developments are leadership and governance facts that investors could price independently of any accounting question.

Commentary has also framed the selloff as a bubble deflating. Ed Yardeni describes an AI bubble "losing some air" rather than bursting, while Paul Krugman has argued a collapse would almost surely cause recession. Those are opinions about the sector, not measurements of the probe's effect, and they should not be merged with the accounting question.
sections.why: Policymakers who treat the SEC report as the cause of the selloff will misread the market and overstate what an unconfirmed inquiry has established.

sections.title: Retirement savers hold more AI risk than they realize
paragraphs: The channel from one company's accounting questions to a saver's account runs through index funds. A broad S&P 500 index fund holds Nvidia in proportion to its market value, so a drop in the stock moves the fund directly, and a drop in a few large AI names moves the whole index. Target-date funds, 401(k) defaults and many pension portfolios hold those same index exposures. A probe of one company therefore reaches people who have never heard of Nvidia's auditors.

Concentration is the real measure, and the numbers carry uncertainty. Bloomberg reported on Nov. 6 that about 44% of US pension fund holdings, roughly $610 billion, were tied up in tech, and that more than half of the S&P 500's gain of about $32 trillion since ChatGPT came from just 10 companies. A separate analysis, from USA Benefits Now and not a primary source, put Nvidia at nearly 8% of the index before the recent drop. Those figures use different baselines and definitions, so officials should cite them as ranges rather than precise shares. What is not in dispute is that a small group of stocks now drives index returns, which means a single company's disclosure problem can move savings at scale.

Public attitudes add a political layer. A University of Michigan preliminary November survey found consumer anxiety tied to a possible AI bubble, though that finding came from open-ended comments without a reported share. Motley Fool's survey of roughly 60% of respondents who were not concerned about an AI slump predates this selloff by about a year and is promotional, so it says little about current sentiment. CNBC's October survey found 63% of respondents did not want an AI data center nearby, and 52% of voters wanted advanced AI development paused until Congress passes safety rules. Those are the voters who will judge how Congress handled the losses in the midterms that just ended.

This is the main domestic stake, and it is larger than the probe itself. Nvidia's accounting questions may prove narrow, as the 2002–03 inquiry did, which closed with no penalty. The bigger question is how much ordinary savings depend on a few AI stocks being accurately reported.
sections.why: a retirement system concentrated in a handful of AI names turns every disclosure question into a household finance question.

sections.title: Enforcement credibility depends on a lighter-touch SEC
paragraphs: The SEC's reported inquiry into Nvidia is a test of whether the agency's stated focus on accounting is substantive or rhetorical. Reuters reported on November 20 that enforcement staff are examining the company's accounting, citing two people briefed on the matter; the SEC declined to comment and has not confirmed a start date or a formal order. Enforcement Director David Woodcock told Reuters in October that the agency was examining AI companies' disclosures, so the Nvidia matter is the first large-cap case that will show whether that statement has teeth.

The 2002–03 precedent cuts both ways. Nvidia's earlier accounting inquiry ended on September 11, 2003 with a no-admit, no-deny cease-and-desist order and no penalty, and the company's 8-K said it had no effect on reported results. That outcome is often read as proof that such probes are survivable. It is also a reminder that the SEC has historically settled large-cap accounting matters on soft terms. Note that the SEC rescinded its no-admit, no-deny policy on May 19, 2026, so any settlement now would likely take a different form.

The agency's own numbers are read in opposite ways. SEC enforcement actions fell to 348 in FY2026 from 456, and public-company actions hit a record low of 16, a 71% drop according to the SEED database. Chair Paul Atkins has said success should not be measured by case counts, and Better Markets' Benjamin Schiffrin asked how "effectiveness" is being measured at all. Cornerstone Research attributes part of the decline to leadership transitions, while White & Case points mainly to staffing shortages, a 43-day shutdown and vacancies. The new financial reporting and accounting unit, launched in August, is either a serious countersignal or a modest one; Foley Hoag cautions that the predecessor task force produced only a small increase in financial reporting cases.

Officials should not assume a case will be brought, nor that a quiet close would prove the SEC's approach is working. The informed reading is that the Nvidia inquiry will be judged on its process and its eventual disclosure, not on whether it produces a headline penalty.
sections.why: if an accounting probe of the country's most valuable chipmaker closes without public findings, the market and Congress will have little basis to judge whether the SEC's lighter-touch posture still protects investors.

sections.title: Implications for U.S. interests and policy options
paragraphs: The most useful lever for policymakers is disclosure, not punishment. Nvidia's 10-Q was due "in the coming weeks" after Nov. 17, and it is the first document that could say whether the SEC inquiry is material to investors. Officials should press the company to state plainly whether it has received an SEC inquiry, what it has disclosed, and whether an independent board committee review is under way. Nvidia has not confirmed the probe. Until it does, no official should describe the probe as a formal case.

Congressional timing matters more than rhetoric. The House chairs have sought transcribed interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and with General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2, with subpoenas threatened, and Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott has asked for Huang on Dec. 3 and Commerce Secretary Lutnick on Dec. 10. Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily. Hearings held before the SEC has said anything public risk turning an unconfirmed inquiry into a partisan spectacle, which Sen. Tillis has already signaled he wants to avoid. Committees should ask the SEC and Nvidia for status briefings in closed session first, and reserve public testimony for matters the agencies can confirm.

Coordination is the harder problem. The SEC is examining accounting, Commerce and DOJ are running the Megaspeed export-control matter, and DOJ is reviewing the $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal, while California's attorney general has subpoenaed the company separately. These tracks have different standards and can pull in opposite directions; one agency's silence can be read as another's cover. Officials should seek a clear statement of which agency leads on which question and whether information is being shared, without suggesting any agency should halt work to suit another.

Retirement-risk guidance is where the public stake sits. Bloomberg estimates roughly $610 billion of pension holdings, about 44%, is tied to tech, and a large share of the S&P 500's gain since ChatGPT came from ten companies. Regulators can ask plan sponsors and index-fund disclosures to make single-name and sector concentration visible, and the Anthropic listing, with possible index inclusion and lock-up sales, adds new supply risk to watch. The tradeoff is that concentration rules could disturb markets and that much of this exposure reflects choices savers made deliberately.

The course that fits the evidence is to demand disclosure, schedule oversight after the facts are on the record, and treat the SEC inquiry as open. The 2002 episode ended in a no-penalty order with neither admission nor denial, and the SEC has since dropped its no-admit-no-deny policy, so any outcome will be judged on its form as well as its findings.
sections.why: policy that assumes guilt before the SEC acts will damage the credibility of the inquiry and the market it is meant to protect.

watch: Nvidia's 10-Q, due in the coming weeks, and whether it discloses the SEC inquiry as a material legal proceeding.
House interviews with Huang on Dec 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec 2, and possible subpoenas.
Senate Banking hearing with Huang on Dec 3 and Lutnick on Dec 10.
Independent board committee findings on the Nvidia investigation, with no date disclosed.
Anthropic lockup expirations and any index-provider inclusion decision, which could shift passive flows.

people.name: Colette M. Kress
people.role: INTERIM CEO AND EXECUTIVE VICE PRESIDENT AND CFO, NVIDIA CORPORATION
people.lede: Kress is the executive whose reported financial numbers sit at the center of the SEC accounting inquiry, and she now holds both the interim CEO and CFO roles while the board searches for a permanent chief. She wants to steady the workforce and investors, keep the company's strategy unchanged, and be seen as a credible steward of its finances.

blocks.heading: Who they are
blocks.text: Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since September 2013 and, since November 12, 2026, its interim CEO after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. Her interim role runs until a permanent successor is named, and she keeps her CFO and executive vice president posts while doing it. Before Nvidia she spent nearly 25 years in finance at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco, and she is a widely known voice on Nvidia's quarterly earnings calls.

blocks.heading: Personality and style
blocks.text: Colleagues and analysts describe her as a calm, numbers-first finance executive, a contrast to Huang's more volatile style. The Wall Street Journal, as cited in her Wikipedia entry, reported that Huang called her "a deer in the headlights" and a "reporting CFO" in an August 2026 meeting, a characterization Huang's side has not been reported to confirm. In her first all-hands meeting, CNBC reported she told staff "let's move forward," and a Yahoo analyst segment said her phrase for the meeting was "we got this." Reuters-based reporting says she was described as having repeatedly questioned the strategy of funding neoclouds, which the briefing treats as a point of internal tension rather than a finding.

blocks.heading: Career highlights
items: 1990s: Began her career in finance roles at Texas Instruments.
About 2000 to 2013: Spent roughly 13 years at Microsoft, including four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division.
2010 to 2013: Served three years as senior vice president and CFO of Cisco's Business Technology and Operations Finance organization.
September 2013: Joined Nvidia as EVP and CFO after a two-year search, when the company was the smallest she had worked for.
November 12, 2026: Named interim CEO after Huang's resignation, while keeping her CFO role.
2026: Ranked #49 on Fortune's Most Powerful Women list.

blocks.heading: Current involvements
items: Interim CEO and EVP and CFO of Nvidia, serving until a permanent successor is named; the board has said it will consider internal and external candidates.

Board's permanent CEO search: the board said on November 13 it was still selecting a search firm and had not formally engaged candidates; it later hired Heidrick & Struggles, according to board chair Harvey Jones's account reported by TweakTown.

Nvidia SEC accounting inquiry: Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues; the opening date and precise focus remain unclear, and Nvidia's position on the inquiry is not reported in the coverage I reviewed.
Independent board committee investigation into her, reported by Axios and tied to the Huang matter; the scope of that review has not been publicly detailed.
Pending 10-Q filing, which Nvidia said would come in the coming weeks, per the briefing's Yahoo/Bloomberg material.

blocks.heading: Big wins
items: Helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth, in the words of board chair Harvey Jones.
Earnings guidance: the briefing reports she projected next-year growth of 75%, with $2.68 adjusted EPS on $115.8 billion in revenue, per Geo TV; the stock fell despite it.
Credited by analysts and the Wikipedia entry with directing Nvidia's AI-era investments and finance digitization, and with a role in the company's rapid rise during the AI boom.
Named a billionaire in July 2025 on the basis of her Nvidia equity, per the encyclopedia entry.

blocks.heading: Controversies
items: Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported an SEC enforcement inquiry into Nvidia's accounting practices; Reuters could not determine when it opened or the precise issues. Nvidia shares fell about 13% on the report. Kress has not been reported as a subject of the inquiry, and the inquiry is unconfirmed.
Governance concern, flagged in the briefing and not a finding: she holds both interim CEO and CFO roles, so financial reporting oversight sits with the executive whose numbers are under review.

Reuters reporting, cited in her encyclopedia entry, says she knew of Huang's relationship with a Nvidia vice president who reported to him; Huang's allegations and the board's handling of them are separate matters.

Her commitment to be more selective in AI financing deals, which she announced on the earnings call, follows her earlier questioning of neocloud funding strategy as reported by Reuters-derived coverage; the connection between the two is contested in coverage and is not established.

blocks.heading: Who they align with
items: Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia board chair, who publicly expressed full confidence in her and said the board does not intend to bring Huang back.
Nvidia's board, which is running a permanent CEO search and has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, according to the Financial Times as reported by Fox Business.
Ian Buck, Nvidia's VP and GM of Hyperscale, who stood beside her at the all-hands meeting and is among internal leaders analysts have named as possible successors.

Jensen Huang, the former CEO and co-founder, whose relationship with her was marked by reported conflict over AI financing deals; Huang's camp has not been reported as supportive of her interim leadership.

Rivals and skeptics: investors and analysts who question whether Nvidia can keep its momentum without Huang, and SEC enforcement staff examining accounting practices, whose work could weigh on her tenure.

people.name: Paul Stewart Atkins
people.role: CHAIRMAN, U.S. SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION (34TH CHAIR, SINCE APRIL 2025)
people.lede: Atkins leads the agency whose accounting inquiry into Nvidia is at the center of this briefing, and whose enforcement posture is under question. He wants a deregulated, more attractive public market, which he has framed as making IPOs great again.

blocks.heading: Who they are
blocks.text: Atkins is a lawyer and former SEC commissioner (2002 to 2008) who returned to the agency as chairman after being confirmed 52-44 on April 9, 2025, and sworn in April 21, 2025. Before returning he ran Patomak Global Partners, a risk-management and compliance consultancy he founded, and he co-chaired the Token Alliance, a crypto advocacy group. The Senate confirmed him for a term expiring June 5, 2026, and a later Senate record shows a reappointment nomination for a term expiring June 5, 2031, confirmed 51-47 on October 7, 2025, which settles his renomination status.

blocks.heading: Personality and style
blocks.text: Public Citizen describes Atkins as presiding over an agency where conflicts of interest have become a requirement for senior leadership, a characterization the group attributes to its researcher Douglas Pasternak. Better Markets' Ben Schiffrin says Atkins wants to cut quarterly reporting in half, while Atkins himself is described by Reuters as keeping a relatively low profile in the administration while advancing its business-friendly agenda. Atkins has said enforcement success should not be measured by case counts, and he has pledged to remain accessible to the regulated community, as in his November 19, 2026 remarks to investment advisers.

blocks.heading: Career highlights
items: 1980: A.B. from Wofford College, Phi Beta Kappa; later J.D. from Vanderbilt Law School in 1983.
1983-1990: Lawyer at Davis Polk & Wardwell in New York, including a 2½-year stint in the Paris office.
1990-1994: Staff to SEC Chairmen Richard Breeden (chief of staff) and Arthur Levitt (counselor).
2002-2008: SEC commissioner, appointed by President George W. Bush and serving under three chairmen.
2009-2010: Member of the Congressional Oversight Panel for the Troubled Asset Relief Program.
2009-2025: Founded and led Patomak Global Partners, a regulatory compliance firm whose clients included Fidelity Investments and Goldman Sachs.
April 21, 2025: Sworn in as the 34th SEC chairman, after Trump nominated him in January 2025.

blocks.heading: Current involvements
items: Chairman of the SEC, with a reappointment nomination for a term to June 5, 2031, confirmed by the Senate in October 2025.

Leading the agency's tokenized-securities Innovation Exemption, issued September 17, 2026, which Senate Democrats Alsobrooks, Gallego, Warner and Cortez Masto have challenged in a November 16 letter demanding answers within 30 days on anti-money laundering gaps.

Overseeing a proposal to cut executive pay disclosure from the top five executives to two, and a broader plan to let companies report earnings twice a year, which critics say would weaken investor information.

Overseeing the Nvidia accounting inquiry, which Reuters reported on November 20, 2026 citing two people briefed on the matter; the SEC has not publicly confirmed it and Atkins has not commented on it in the reporting I reviewed.
Pending oversight of the SEC's Enforcement Division, where David Woodcock is director and a new financial reporting and accounting unit was recently launched.

blocks.heading: Big wins
items: Confirmed by the Senate in April 2025 by a 52-44 vote, and then reconfirmed for a term to 2031 by a 51-47 vote in October 2025.
Secured the SEC's September 2026 Innovation Exemption allowing qualifying venues to trade tokenized U.S. stocks for five years, a move he has tied to his capital-markets agenda.
Advanced a deregulatory agenda that supporters, including Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, have credited with providing regulatory clarity for digital assets and promoting capital formation.

blocks.heading: Controversies
items: Public Citizen says Atkins's SEC has a dozen senior officials with apparent or potential conflicts of interest, and that enforcement actions against several of Atkins's former clients were dropped soon after he arrived.

Better Markets' Ben Schiffrin says Atkins wants to cut quarterly reporting in half and questioned how the SEC measures effectiveness, while over 200,000 public comments, mostly from investors, opposed the optional quarterly-reporting measure.

At the time of his appointment Atkins owned about $6 million in crypto-related holdings and pledged to divest; Wikipedia reports later filings did not list those businesses, a point I could not verify against primary filings, and sources conflict on whether divestment was fully disclosed.
Enforcement actions fell to 348 in FY2026 from 456, and public-company actions hit a record low of 16 per the SEED database, a 71% drop, which critics say weakens oversight.

blocks.heading: Who they align with
items: Patrons and allies: President Donald Trump, who nominated him, and Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, who backed his confirmation.
Fellow commissioners Mark Uyeda, Hester Peirce, and Kristin Johnson's nomination, with Peirce leading the Crypto Task Force.
Industry backers: the crypto and digital-asset sector, including the Digital Chamber's Token Alliance, and business groups such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a former Patomak client.
Rivals: Senate Democrats Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto, who have challenged the tokenization exemption.
Rivals: Better Markets, led on securities policy by Ben Schiffrin, and Public Citizen, which have criticized his enforcement and conflict-of-interest record.
